extracted.intended_audience: writers, students of rhetoric, and classical literature scholars interested in producing or evaluating elevated prose style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating the 'elevated' or sublime prose style: what diction, figures, word-order, particles, sound-patterns, and subject-matter choices make prose lofty, and what misuse or excesses to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid smoothness and evenness in elevated style
rubrics_metrics.description: In the elevated style smoothness and pleasant cadences have no place; Thucydides almost invariably avoids smoothness and evenness of composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rugged, stumbling air (as travellers on rough roads) can increase effectiveness; e.g., reversing an obviously 'euphonious' order may preserve force (‘by common consent, this year was free from other maladies’ vs the more effective original order). Smoothness that reduces force is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rugged/augmented words to assimilate to composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition makes style impressive in the same way as a rugged word does: use stronger/augmented words (e.g., 'shrieking' in place of 'crying,' 'bursting' in place of 'charging').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select verbs/adjectives that match the energy of the composition; assimilate words to composition and composition to words for heightened effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order elements by ascending vividness
rubrics_metrics.description: First should be placed those that are not so vivid; in the second or last place should come those that are distinctly so, so that what follows is more vivid still.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to increase vividness (i.e., having the order lapse from strength to weakness) loses vigour. Example: Plato's phrasing where the second expression is more vivid than the first; reverse ordering would weaken impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Augment hyperbole progressively
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyperbole should be augmented continuously so the scale mounts higher and higher (Homer's description of the Cyclops).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build cumulative exaggeration rather than throwing in a single, disconnected superlative; progressive augmentation intensifies grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive nicety in connectives (some negligence desirable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Connectives such as πέv and δέ should not correspond too nicely; there is something trivial in excessive nicety. A certain negligence in the use of particles is desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate irregularity or loose matching of particles can lend dignity or grandeur; slavish, mechanical correspondence among particles is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce expletive/contrast particles only when they add dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Expletive particles must not be employed as pointless appendages; they must be introduced only if they contribute something to dignity of style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Lo!', 'Ah me!', 'Alas!' etc., when they add feeling or sever what follows from what precedes; inserting particles aimlessly (as actors adding cries without reason) is a misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of particle near sentence-beginning can dignify
rubrics_metrics.description: A particle placed near the beginning, severing what follows from what precedes, makes a dignified impression; amplified beginnings have a stately effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position particles to create a pause/separation that amplifies the following clause (examples from Plato and Homer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign figures of speech to style (use appropriate figures for elevated style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures of speech are themselves a form of composition and specific figures should be assigned to the elevated style (e.g., anthypallage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose figures that suit the elevated register rather than using the same figures across all styles indiscriminately; the appropriate figures must be assigned to each several style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use anthypallage and similar figures for stateliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Anthypallage (substitution of grammatical case or shifting modifier relationships) produces a more stately effect than the ordinary way of phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'And the twin rocks—one of the twain with its peak towers up to the skies' is more stately than the ordinary construction; ordinary phrasing is trivial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repetition and disjunction to magnify small things
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of names and avoidance of conjunctions gives an impression of copious power even for small items (e.g., Nireus repeated three times).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recurrence to the same name and omission of conjunctions creates an impression of multitude and importance; this is an elevating device when used tactfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repeated conjunctions (combination) to suggest multitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Combination by repeating the same conjunction (e.g., 'both Greeks and Carians and Lycians...') gives the impression of an innumerable host.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast: repetition of conjunctions creates multiplicity; omission of conjunctions creates distinction—use each effect intentionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit conjunctions for distinction (parataxis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of 'and' in phrases like 'high-arched, foam-crested' lends an air of greater distinction than inserting the conjunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parataxis can increase distinction and elevation; inserting conjunctions where not needed can blunt the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary sentence construction to increase strikingness
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not keep to the same construction; varied construction (as in Thucydides' sequence) is far more striking than retaining the same grammatical structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence actions and vary clause types to create momentum and surprise rather than monotony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redouble words (repetition) to impart impressiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Redoubling a word (repeating it) can impart impressiveness to the style (e.g., 'huge species—a big species, and a lot of them').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactical repetition enhances emphasis; avoid accidental or purposeless repetition which signals weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overloading with figures of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Overloading with figures should be avoided, as it betokens lack of taste and produces inequality of style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancients use many figures artistically; excessive, clumsy accumulation of figures is an anti-pattern—use figures skillfully and sparingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage concurrence of vowels (hiatus) with taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Concurrence of vowels: the composition should not 'clang' from inartistic collisions, nor should vowel contact be shunned altogether; the true course lies between extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isocrates avoided vowel concurrence; others embrace it. Avoid jerkiness from careless vowel collisions but allow musical vowel combinations where tasteful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concurrence of long vowels and diphthongs to elevate rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: The concurrence of long vowels (and diphthongs) is especially appropriate in the elevated style; hiatus can lengthen a line and reproduce a mighty heaviness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: lines where hiatus reproduces the 'heaving' of a stone or the labour of an action; deliberate vowel patterns can add musical heft to elevated passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use subject-matter of large scope to produce elevation
rubrics_metrics.description: Elevation resides also in the nature of the subject-matter (great and famous battles, earth, heaven); the subject itself contributes to the listener's impression that the style is great.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose expansive themes (naval battles, cavalry engagements) that offer grand representations; caveat—great topics can be handled meanly, so method of narration remains crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction should be superior, distinguished, and somewhat unfamiliar
rubrics_metrics.description: The diction employed in the elevated style should be superior, distinguished, and inclined to the unfamiliar; usual and current words, though clear, are unimpressive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select words that lend gravity; avoid common quotidian terms that may cheapen the elevated register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metaphors in prose, but sparingly and naturally
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphors must be used in prose style because they impart charm and grandeur, but they should not be crowded together nor far-fetched; they should be natural and based on a true analogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer metaphors grounded in clear analogy (e.g., general/pilot/charioteer analogies). Excessive or strained metaphors risk turning prose into dithyrambic poetry or triviality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert daring metaphors into similes for safety
rubrics_metrics.description: When the metaphor seems daring, convert it into a simile for greater security ('the orator was like a flood rushing upon you').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similes expand metaphors and reduce risk; Plato often prefers metaphor (riskier), Xenophon prefers simile (safer). Choose according to desired boldness and audience tolerance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'active' metaphors that animate inanimate things
rubrics_metrics.description: Active metaphor—introducing inanimate things in a state of activity as though animate—is judged best (Aristotle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Sharp-shot flies at the crowd the angry shaft'; 'foam-crested' or 'the battle shuddered'—these animate the scene and intensify imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metaphors when they increase clarity and precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Some things are expressed with greater clearness and precision by metaphors than by precise literal terms (e.g., 'the battle shuddered').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a metaphor conveys the phenomenon more truthfully and vividly than literal phrasing, it is preferable; retain metaphors that increase comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid trivial or far-fetched metaphors that diminish grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: Some metaphors conduce to triviality rather than grandeur even though employed to enhance effect; such metaphors are to be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for metaphors that feel cheap, forced, or ludicrous—these are anti-patterns that undermine elevated style.
